newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper takes new swipe at U.S.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper takes new swipe at U.S.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper called for a truce in Colombia's war of words with Washington on Tuesday, but he took a swipe at U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette and continued to criticise U.S. drug policy.

In a speech at the Casa de Narino presidential palace, Samper said there was "an understandable sense of national frustration" after the recent U.S. decision to "decertify" Colombia as a trusthworthy ally in the war on drugs.
"The country was right to be enraged ... because this decision was as injust as it was demoralising," he said, referring to a recent surge in anti-American rhetoric and verbal attacks on Frechette.

Samper said Frechette had brought some of that anger on himself and had been "diplomatically reprimanded" for stepping out of line. "Without respecting the pain that the (decertification) decision caused, the U.S. ambassador threw down the gauntlet a few hours after it was announced by talking about new conditions and demands that clearly reignited already offended tempers," Samper said.

He did not elaborate but the outspoken diplomat called for the lifting of Colombia's constitutional ban on extradition in television and newspaper interviews shortly after the certification decision was announced. He also said for the first time that two major drug lords had offered to provide him with evidence of Samper's alleged tries to the drug trade.

Allegations that Samper received millions of dollars in drug money to finance his 1994 campaign have been cited by U.S. officials a reason for the Feb. 28 decision to leave Colombia on a drugs blacklist for a second consecutive year. The decision, which outraged many Colombians, left Latin America's oldest democracy on a list of virtual outlaw states that have failed to do enough to fight drugs.

Frechette was dubbed a "sick gringo" over the weekend by Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, Samper's right-hand man, and called a "son-of-a-bitch" by Jaime Dussan, a senator with close ties to the president. Those attacks and others prompted Frechette to complain to reporters on Monday that he was concered about his personal safety.

Samper said it was time to call a truce in the "war of declarations" between Bogota and Washington. "It falls to all of us, without exception, to lower the discussion volume while we continue working for Colombia," he said.
Dussan, who was on hand for the speech, was not convinced. "This gringo (Frechette) has all the power in the world and now he says he feels threatened," he told reporters.
"This is like a poor mouse getting into a fight with a lion ... if he's such a coward we should get him out of here all that much sooner," Dussan added.

Meanwhile, congressman Carlos Alonso Lucio, a former member of Colombia's disbanded M-19 guerrilla movement, told Reuters he had drafted legislation that would allow Samper to nationalise U.S. businesses in Colombia if Washington imposed economic sanctions on the country because of its perceived failure to win the drug war.
